content: Acne, medically known as acne vulgaris, is a common chronic skin condition characterized by the formation of pimples, blackheads, whiteheads (comedones), and sometimes cysts mainly on areas with high concentrations of sebaceous (oil) glands such as the face, back, and chest. Acne develops primarily due to blockage and inflammation of hair follicles caused by excess sebum production, abnormal shedding of skin cells (keratin), Propionibacterium acnes bacterial colonization, and inflammation. Hormonal influences, genetics, and environmental factors contribute to its onset and severity. Practically, acne can affect individuals of all ages but is most prevalent in adolescents and young adults and may cause physical discomfort and psychological distress including lowered self-esteem and social anxiety. Common synonyms include "pimples," "zits," "spots," and "blemishes." Although many treatment options exist such as topical retinoids, benzoyl peroxide, antibiotics, hormonal therapy, and procedural interventions, limitations include variable efficacy, potential side effects like skin irritation or antibiotic resistance, and the chronic recurrent nature of acne. Safety considerations emphasize guided use of medications and avoidance of unproven or harmful remedies. Knowledge about acne and its management empowers patients and caregivers to seek proper evaluation and adopt effective treatment and lifestyle modifications to improve skin health and quality of life.

chunk_title: What is Acne? Definition and Types
content: Acne (acne vulgaris) is a chronic skin disorder involving inflammation of the pilosebaceous units. It manifests through a spectrum of lesions—comedones (non-inflammatory; blackheads and whiteheads), inflammatory papules, pustules, nodules, and cysts. Acne lesions commonly appear on the face, neck, chest, upper back, and shoulders due to dense sebaceous gland distribution.

chunk_title: Causes and Risk Factors of Acne
content: The main causes include increased sebum production from sebaceous glands, abnormal keratinization blocking hair follicles, colonization by Cutibacterium acnes (formerly Propionibacterium acnes), and inflammation. Risk factors involve hormonal changes (e.g., puberty, menstrual cycles), genetic predisposition, certain medications (steroids, lithium), diet (high glycemic load, dairy), stress, and environmental exposures such as humidity and occlusive cosmetics.

content: Acne develops via interplay of increased androgen levels stimulating sebaceous glands, follicular hyperkeratinization causing clogged pores, bacterial proliferation leading to immune response (mainly by Cutibacterium acnes), and subsequent inflammation. This cascade results in visible skin lesions and, in severe cases, tissue scarring.

content: Acne presents as various lesions: non-inflammatory (comedones - blackheads and whiteheads) and inflammatory (papules, pustules, nodules, cysts). Symptoms may include redness, swelling, tenderness, and sometimes pain. Severity ranges from mild with few lesions to severe cystic acne causing scarring and significant discomfort.

chunk_title: When and How to Seek Medical Evaluation
content: Consult a healthcare provider if acne is moderate to severe, persistent despite over-the-counter treatments, causes scarring, psychological distress, or if symptoms worsen rapidly. Dermatologic evaluation can help tailor treatment strategies, assess for underlying causes, and prevent complications.

review_status: AI draft - scientific, clinical, and editorial review required
content: Treatment depends on acne severity. Mild acne often improves with topical therapies like benzoyl peroxide, retinoids, and antibiotics. Moderate-to-severe cases may require oral antibiotics, hormonal therapy (e.g., oral contraceptives, anti-androgens), or isotretinoin. Procedural options include chemical peels, laser therapy, and drainage of cysts. Treatment adherence and follow-up are important for success.

chunk_title: Role of Lifestyle and Dietary Considerations
content: Lifestyle factors such as gentle skin cleansing twice daily, avoiding harsh scrubbing, non-comedogenic skincare products, stress management, and adequate sleep may benefit acne control. Emerging evidence suggests that reducing high glycemic index foods and certain dairy products may improve acne, although definitive consensus is lacking.

content: Myths include that acne is caused by poor hygiene, dirt, or contagious infection. Contrary to some beliefs, squeezing or popping pimples can worsen inflammation and cause scarring. Acne is influenced by complex hormonal and genetic factors, not simply skin cleanliness.

chunk_title: Limitations and Side Effects of Acne Treatments
content: Topical treatments may cause skin irritation, dryness, or photosensitivity. Oral antibiotics can lead to resistance or gastrointestinal upset. Isotretinoin carries risks of teratogenicity and requires careful monitoring. Treatment responses vary; no single therapy guarantees complete cure, and recurrence is common.
